When no current passed through the wire, under the action of the geomagnetic field, the N pole of the small magnetic needle pointed north when it was at rest, as shown in the figure. Now a constant current I from south to north passes through the wire. After the small magnetic needle turns and comes to rest again, its N pole points

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left side of the figure is a long straight wire placed horizontally. Above the wire is marked current I, with the arrow pointing to the right; directly below the wire is a small magnetic needle, with the S pole on the left and the N pole on the right. The direction marker on the right shows that to the right in the figure is north and to the left is south, so the current direction in the figure is from south to north, and the N pole of the small magnetic needle originally pointed north. Then reason: when there is no current, the small magnetic needle is acted on only by the geomagnetic field, and the N pole points north, indicating that the original geomagnetic field direction is taken as north. After current is passed, the long straight wire produces an additional magnetic field at the small magnetic needle. According to the right-hand screw rule, the thumb points along the current direction, namely from south to north, and the direction in which the four fingers curl gives the magnetic field direction; at the position of the small magnetic needle directly below the wire, the magnetic field produced by the current points west. The small magnetic needle finally comes to rest along the direction of the resultant magnetic field, namely the resultant direction of the geomagnetic field toward north and the current magnetic field toward west, so the N pole finally points in a direction west of north. Final answer: in a direction west of north.
